title: The trustworthy
hook: Mecca calls him al-Amin and al-Sadiq, the trustworthy and the truthful

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fudul, the pact of the wronged. Your line was: defend the wronged. Did you take your small step for someone treated unfairly? Day seven hundred fifteen.

Some reputations are built by speeches. This one, as the sirah tells it, was built the slow way, in the ordinary dealings of a trading town: what a person says, what a person keeps, what a person gives back. By the time the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a grown man in Mecca, the sirah says, people have stopped using only his name. They call him by what he is to them. A title given not by a king, but by neighbors and traders. Today: the trustworthy.
screen: `NOT BUILT BY SPEECHES.` → `SMALL THINGS, DONE THE SAME WAY.` → `A TITLE FROM THE NEIGHBORS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq says Quraysh called him al-Amin, the trustworthy. Tradition remembers him too as al-Sadiq, the truthful. Two words, one picture: a man whose word matched what happened, and whose hands could be trusted with what wasn't his. Muslims often point to two hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari where the praise comes from people who had turned against his message. The first comes from the day he began to call his own clans in public. He climbs the hill of Safa and calls them by name. When they gather, he asks: if I told you there were horsemen in the valley behind this hill, about to attack you, would you believe me? And they answer: yes, we have never known you to say anything but the truth. Then he tells them his message, and his own uncle Abu Lahab scolds him in front of everyone. But they had already said it. The second comes from Abu Sufyan, at the time still one of his fiercest opponents, standing before the Byzantine emperor Heraclius, who questions him about this new prophet. Heraclius asks: did you ever accuse him of lying, before he made his claim? And Abu Sufyan says no. In the same report he admits he'd have lied about him if he hadn't feared his companions calling him a liar. Heraclius reasons aloud: a man who never lied about people would hardly lie about God. Both scenes come from after the revelation began, but both look back. In them, even his opponents say that before the message, they had known him for his word. The trust was there first.
screen: `AL-AMIN AND AL-SADIQ.` · `"WOULD YOU BELIEVE ME?" AT SAFA.` · `ABU SUFYAN BEFORE HERACLIUS.` · `THE TRUST CAME FIRST.` · then, large: `KNOWN FOR TRUTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: be truthful in one hard moment. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a moment coming up today or this week where the easy thing is a small untruth. An excuse for being late. A compliment you don't mean. A number rounded the convenient way. Picture the moment clearly. Now picture yourself saying the true thing instead, kindly, plainly. Notice what happens in your body. Rehearse the sentence once in your head until it feels like yours. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make your word match your deed. The bell holds the time.
The trustworthy. Al-Amin, what Mecca called him, the sirah says, before any revelation came, and al-Sadiq, the truthful. Today's word.
Your line: known for truth. Today, when the hard moment you rehearsed arrives, say the true sentence, kindly. Day seven hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Muslims refer to the Prophet ﷺ as al-Sadiq al-Amin, the truthful and trustworthy, and honesty in speech and trade is taught as part of following his example.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Quraysh called him al-Amin)

notes: Ibn Ishaq attests al-Amin; al-Sadiq is given as tradition's title ('tradition remembers him too as'). Confirm sourcing.

The Safa scene and Abu Sufyan's interview come after the start of revelation; the script uses them as witnesses to an earlier reputation and says so. Confirm this does not teach later events out of place.
The teach and fork reveal mention only Abu Lahab's rebuke, which Bukhari 4770 records; confirm.
Bukhari numbers 4770 and 7 cited from memory; confirm.
The hook's 'built the slow way' framing is the writer's summary of the sirah, not a quoted source.
The Black Stone episode (where Quraysh say 'here is al-Amin') is not told here, to leave it for its own day.

Auditor: the teach had the narrator argue 'how do we know the reputation was real' and close with 'the question wasn't whether he lied, it was what to do if he didn't', which is apologetics in the narrator's voice and overstates the case (the Qur'an itself records opponents calling him a liar, e.g. 38:4). Now attributed ('Muslims often point to'), Abu Sufyan's own admission from Bukhari 7 replaces 'who'd have loved to say yes', and the close stays with what the reports say.
